cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Spoilage & Microorganisms
cards.back: Food spoilage is caused by microorganisms (bacteria, yeasts, moulds) breaking down food.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Spoilage & Microorganisms
cards.back: Bacteria are the most common cause of food spoilage and food-borne illness.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Spoilage & Microorganisms
cards.back: Yeasts cause fermentation, producing alcohol and carbon dioxide — useful in bread-making but spoilage in other foods.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Spoilage & Microorganisms
cards.back: Moulds grow as visible fuzzy patches and can produce harmful mycotoxins.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Spoilage & Microorganisms
cards.back: The conditions microorganisms need to grow are summarised by FATTOM: Food, Acidity, Temperature, Time, Oxygen, Moisture.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Spoilage & Microorganisms
cards.back: The danger zone for bacterial growth is 5°C to 63°C; bacteria multiply fastest at around 37°C.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Spoilage & Microorganisms
cards.back: Signs of spoilage include: unpleasant smell, discolouration, slime, visible mould, gas bubbles, off-taste.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Spoilage & Microorganisms
cards.back: Enzymatic browning and oxidation are chemical changes (not microbial) that also spoil food appearance and quality.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Spoilage & Microorganisms
cards.back: Freezing at −18°C stops microbial growth but does not kill bacteria; they reactivate when thawed.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Food Spoilage & Microorganisms
cards.back: Pasteurisation heats food to 72°C for 15 seconds, killing most harmful bacteria without destroying flavour.

cards.front: What should you know about food preparation & nutrition exam tips — food spoilage & microorganisms?
cards.back: 1. For Food Spoilage & Microorganisms questions, show every step of your working clearly — method marks count even if the final answer is wrong 2. Check your answer makes sense in context (estimation, units, reasonableness) 3. Use correct mathematical notation and state formulae before substituting values 4. If a Food Spoilage & Microorganisms question asks you to 'prove' or 'show', write a logical chain of reasoning with a conclusion line 5. For problem-solving, identify the topic first, then recall the relevant method
